Capital punishment has undergone an interesting cultural evolution since the medieval ages. Back then, capital punishment would have been one big spectacle - the criminal would be displayed in front of a great crowd and often would be forced to undergo a long and excruciatingly painful death (by being put on the wheel, drawn and quartered, gutted, etc., etc.) before expiring. Even those who were not subjected to capital punishment had to undergo ritualized and degrading treatment (i.e., thieves had one of their hands hacked off) that permanently ruined their existence.

With the enlightenment era, lawmakers and philosophers increasingly came to believe that such punishment primarily was an instrument of pointless vengeance, when the actual use of the legal system should be to protect law-abiding citizens. Social rehabilitation of prisoners - so far as possible - rather than permanently making them social outcasts with maimed bodies became the priority, and the capital punishment increasingly became detached from the gory, public spectacle it used to be: Long-winded torture sequences turned into quick and (relatively) painless beheadings via axe or guillotine, and rather than presenting the moribund prisoners in front of a crowd, the execution process was hidden from public view behind the thick walls of a prison.

Bluntly speaking, modern capital punishment is only applied to those who are deemed beyond repair and too much of a publich threat to walk free, and even then, the state wants to remove the killing from the killing process as much as possible. Without the ability to simply sniff out the life of the prisoner with a flick of the fingers, death via poisoning is just about the most visually harmless death available, whereas electrocution and death by firing squad still can be fairly graphic.

In some ways, it may be argued that the modern state, rather than glorifying the killing of its own criminal citizens, actually is ashamed of the fact that it can produce citizens which need to be killed, and as such masks the act of killing as much as possible.
